headline: High-risk filesystem and action overlap: OpenHands can write, browse, and use MCP while marker is a document processor with no isolation guarantees.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read runtime files and use MCP, so if marker outputs are placed in the shared mounted volume, OpenHands may ingest them as instructions. marker itself has no filesystem or MCP surfaces, so the pathway is one-way and depends on shared files rather than direct channeling.
conditions: IF marker outputs are copied into OpenHands's mounted runtime files
IF OpenHands parses those files as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Keep marker outputs in a separate, read-only directory
Disable MCP servers for the OpenHands run
Require a human review step before OpenHands reads marker-generated files
Prefix marker outputs with a non-executable wrapper and strip directives
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between producer and consumer

B_data_leakage.rationale: marker is document-processing and OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime while also having broad network egress. If sensitive documents are mounted into the shared workspace, OpenHands can read and transmit them; marker does not itself show egress, so the leakage risk is driven by OpenHands's default runtime access.
conditions: IF sensitive documents are mounted into OpenHands's runtime sandbox
IF OpenHands sends file contents to its configured model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Mount only the minimum necessary files into OpenHands
Remove secrets and regulated data before sharing the workspace
Use a local model provider with no external egress
Turn off MCP servers for the session
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad runtime actions; marker's profile shows no write or shell capability, so the conflict is asymmetric but still dangerous when both operate on the same mounted volume or repo. Concurrent edits can overwrite files or git state without locking, and the rubric treats shared unrestricted writes as high risk.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory or git repository
IF OpenHands and marker run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Pause one agent before the other writes
Avoid git operations during parallel runs
Use a lock file around shared outputs
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can act on files and browser outputs, so if it consumes marker's extracted text as authoritative, errors can cascade into edits or actions. marker is a document processor and does not verify downstream actions, while OpenHands's agent loop can operationalize its inputs; the pathway exists but is not inherently automatic.
conditions: IF OpenHands treats marker output as ground truth without verification
IF OpenHands uses that output to edit files, browse, or trigger MCP actions
mitigations: Require citation or source checks before acting on marker output
Insert a human approval gate for edits and external actions
Compare marker output against the original document before use
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis when consuming marker output
requires-engineering: add automated verification of extracted facts

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for marker, while OpenHands handles files in its runtime and model-provider keys. The only concrete compliance concern is that shared mounted files could include regulated data, but the profiles do not show a specific cross-border or certification conflict, so the risk stays low.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands's runtime
IF the configured model provider or runtime policy lacks the required compliance controls
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared runtime
Use a provider with the needed compliance posture
Review retention settings before the run
Store secrets outside the workspace
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
